  MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  February 10, 2025
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:02 p.m., on Monday, February 10, 2025, the Alhambra City Council met in the
Council Chambers of Alhambra City Hall.

PRESENT:  LEE, MALONEY, ANDRADE-STADLER, MAZA, WANG
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present: City Manager Binnquist, Assistant City Manager Garcia, Deputy City Manager
Hembree, City Attorney Montes, City Clerk Myles, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias, Director
of Finance Lieu, Director of Community Development Ho, Director of Public Works and Utilities Ahlen,
Chief of Police Kennedy, Chief of Fire Department Ragusa, Director of Library Services LohGuan,
Director of Human Resources Ko, Manager Analyst Alvarez, Public Information Specialist Rodriguez

FLAG SALUTE:  Mayor Wang

LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: We acknowledge that the land on which we are gathered is the
traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Gabrielino/Tongva peoples. We seek to prioritize
respect for the historic culture and contemporary presence of the native peoples throughout California,
especially in the greater Los Angeles/Alhambra area. We come with respect and gratitude for the
Gabrielino/Tongva people who still consider themselves the caretakers of this land. It is through their
examples that we are reminded of our greater responsibility to take care of Mother Earth and to take
care of each other.

PUBLIC COMMENT FOR NON-AGENDIZED ITEMS – F2M25-4
1) Connie M. CERVANTES, 2038 S.Second St., spoke regarding street parking on Second and Hellman
  and the overcrowding which prevents street cleaning. She stated that the medical business at the
  location was causing parking issues and left trash in the street.

2) Valerie MEYER, 824 N. Marguerita Ave., spoke regarding excessive speeding on her street and
  requested action from the City such as speed bumps. She continued to speak regarding excessive
  speeding on residential streets and the threats posed to pedestrians and especially children.

3) Erin MALONEY, 823 N. Marguerita Ave., spoke regarding excessive speeding on her street and
  requested more speed bumps in the area. She referred to the traffic mitigation policy and asked for
  more help from the City. She also asked for an emergency program for more localized contact groups
  within neighborhoods.

4) Gina GARCIA, 819 N. Marguerita Ave., thanked First Responders for their work and went on to speak
  regarding the need for speed bumps on her street to protect children. She requested more information
  regarding the ongoing development of a Traffic Calming policy. She discussed alternative traffic
  calming measures for consideration as well as speed bumps. Ms. GARCIA went on to discuss Hazard
  Mitigation Plan and necessary upgrades to infrastructure.

5) Andrew SEETO, 1846 S. Marguerita Ave., spoke regarding the state of the alleyway behind his home
  and requested the City repair the alley, citing the stress from trash trucks and traffic. He discussed the
  potential dangers of allowing the alley to fall further into disrepair.

  1
2-10-25
 6) Jeffrey GOMEZ discussed the stop sign at Alhambra Road, Electric Avenue and Marengo. He
  distributed photos to Council for reference. He requested the City review the intersection and make
  appropriate updates.

7) Melissa MICHELSON requested Council reform the City Boards and Commissions and practice better
  governance. She went on to discuss challenges faced by the Historic Preservation Commission,
  Environmental Sustainability Commission, City Arts and Cultural Events Commission, and the
  Transportation Commission. She discussed the cancellation of meetings and the agendas as
  assembled by staff. She requested that Commissioners be allowed to add items to the agenda. She
  further discussed the Brown Act and Rosenburg’s Rules of Order and the methods to add items to an
  agenda. She requested an independent investigation into the meetings and ways in which staff enforce
  the bylaws of each Commission.

8) Lewis MCCAMMON, 105 N. Cordova St., discussed the Closed Session agenda regarding property at
  840 S. Almansor St. He went on to discuss the City’s stance on issues of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion.
  He discussed historical national issues of racism, immigration, citizenship and segregation.

WANG:  Mayor WANG thanked the public for their comments, and clarified that although the
Council was not able to respond directly, staff was taking notes and comments were all taken into
account. She stated that Council may make comments relevant to comments during Council
Communications. She stated that Public Comment for Non-Agendized Items would continue at the
end of the meeting.

PRESENTATIONS

1.  RESULTS OF COMMUNITY SATISFACTION SURVEY – F2M24-33

  Public Information Specialist RODRIGUEZ introduced Tim McLARNEY, from True North
  Research who delivered the presentation. The presentation is on file in the City Clerk’s office.
  As part of the Strategic Plan, the City Council prioritized community engagement and
  information. In 2024, staff moved forward with engaging a professional consultant to conduct
  a Community Satisfaction Survey, particularly in advance of the City’s new Strategic Plan and
  new Fiscal Year Budget. The purpose of the Community Satisfaction Survey is to obtain
  statistically reliable data to improve the City’s understanding of the residents’ satisfaction,
  priorities, and concerns as they relate to services, facilities, and policies provided by the City.
  The City engaged True North Research to design the research plan and conduct the City’s
  survey. This will be the third satisfaction survey pursued by the City over the last five years.
  The survey provides opportunity to analyze the City’s progress with services and/or to
  understand top of mind community priorities.

  True North is a full-service survey research firm dedicated to providing agencies with
  understanding of community perceptions, concerns, and priorities. The firm has conducted
  over 1,200 survey research studies for more than 400 cities and school districts. Alhambra’s
  Community Satisfaction Survey was broadly defined and designed to help identify: key
  resident issues; satisfaction with City services; opinions on strategic topics; satisfaction with
  communications and engagement; and other background and demographic data to
  understand needs, perceptions, and interests. Representatives from True North Research will
  present to the City Council details regarding the results of the Community Satisfaction Survey.
  The full detailed results of the survey are featured in the final report prepared by True North,
  which is available on the City’s website.

  Public Comment:
  1) Veronica ALVAREZ, 1833 S. Olive Ave., stated that she did not know about the survey despite
  being an active and long-time resident. She spoke regarding the small sample size, disagreed

  2
2-10-25
   with the premise of the survey, her own history in seeking City assistance regarding tree service
  and the lack of response.

  2) Lewis McCAMMON, 105 N. Cordova St., spoke regarding the survey document, distributed
  handouts of graphs from the survey, which are on file in the City Clerk’s Office, and discussed
  the results regarding satisfaction of services and resident’s service needs and priorities matrix.

  3) Bernice ORTEGA, 227 S. El Molino St., stated that she also did not receive the survey and
  was not aware of the survey. She stated that the questions were not specific enough and that
  the money used for the contracted survey could have been used for other projects. She
  requested an itemized invoice from the contractor and suggested that the contracts for various
  projects needed to be audited and provide additional information to the public.

  Discussion: Council thanked staff and consultants for their work. Councilmember
  MALONEY and Mr. McLARNEY responded to public comments regarding the sample size for
  the survey and the metrics used. They continued to discuss the strategic priorities for next
  year and the language used regarding the improvements to bike lanes question.
  Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER and Mr. McLARNEY discussed the number of
  languages translated and the linguistic sample sizes. Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER discussed
  True North’s knowledge and experience in the City, the upcoming Strategic Plan, and concerns
  regarding internet accessibility for some residents. Vice Mayor LEE and Mr. McLARNEY
  compared and discussed the 2021 and 2022 Community Satisfaction Survey in relation to the
  2025 Community Satisfaction Survey. They continued to discuss questions regarding
  preference for information distribution with regards to social media, email, and direct mail.
  Mayor WANG also discussed email as the preferred method of communication with the public.
  Ms. WANG and Mr. McLARNEY went on to discuss how various public bias were addressed
  in the survey. Ms. WANG suggested more creativity when soliciting responses and educating
  the public regarding the survey. She suggested City booths at various events as well as more
  descriptions in the emailed link.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the 2024 Community Satisfaction Survey.

2.  2024 CITY ACCOMPLISHMENTS REPORT – F2M24-33

  Public Information Specialist RODRIGUEZ outlined the 2024 Accomplishments Report which
  highlights many of the past year’s achievements. The accomplishments aligned with the City’s
  Strategic Plan, which was prioritized to reflect the community’s core values. The Report was
  intended to heighten community awareness of new and ongoing activities and projects. The
  presentation is on file in the City Clerk’s office.

  Discussion:  Council thanked staff for the presentation and for their continued hard work.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and filed the informational report.

3.  HISTORIC PRESERVATION COMMISSION – F2M20-51

  City Manager BINNQUIST delivered a staff report. Over the past few months, the Historic
  Preservation Commission (HPC) has worked on reviewing the Draft Historic Preservation
  Ordinance. During the course of this work, some Commissioners have raised certain issues.
  Staff presented responses based upon staff’s understanding of the City’s Council’s
  expectations for the creation of a Historic Preservation Ordinance, and operation of the HPC
  with respect to: Request to Revisit Historic Context Statement (Phase I) and Historic
  Resources Survey (Phase II); Adding Items to the Commission Agenda and Providing
  Direction to Staff; Providing Links for Virtual Meetings; Moving Public Comment to the
  3
2-10-25
   Beginning of the Agenda; and Pre-meeting Calls. Additionally, since the HPC meeting on
  January 22, 2025, Historic Resources Group contacted staff to discuss the project budget.
  Due to the level of detail required by the Commission, the additional time spent preparing for,
  and attending meetings has impacted costs. Staff anticipated presenting a contract
  amendment to the Council requesting an increase in the budget in order to complete the
  project.

  Public Comment:
  1) Bernice ORTEGA, 227 S. El Molino St., spoke regarding the importance of the Historic
  Preservation Ordinance and the need to take time in crafting the best ordinance. She stated
  that there was no rush and that the Historic Preservation Commission should work directly with
  the Design Review Board and not City staff. She went on to state that staff and the consulting
  firm got in the way.

  2) Bert NG, 203 S. Cordova St., representing the Historic Preservation Commission, spoke
  regarding the items listed in the staff report. He discussed the different phases of the ordinance
  and cautioned against revisiting the phases which have been completed. He went on to discuss
  criticism from a fellow Commissioner who stated that properties had been left out of the Phase
  II Historic Resources Survey, but added that this did not warrant revisiting the phase. He
  discussed the methods built into the ordinance to add additional properties not included in the
  first survey. He also discussed the issue of Commissioners adding items to the meeting
  agenda, and requested further clarification from Council. He supported adding virtual access
  to meetings during discussion of the Historic Preservation ordinance, but that Zoom meetings
  would not be necessary once the regular meetings begin. He supported moving public
  comment to the beginning of the meeting as long as this was the practice for all other Boards
  and Commissions. He further discussed pre-meeting calls and supported this practice over
  email communications.

  3) Jennifer NG, 203 S. Cordova St., discussed Phase I of the Historic Context Survey which was
  accepted by City Council and the move to Phase II. She stated that previous phases did not
  need to be revisited. She discussed the protections offered by the ordinance to include other
  properties and the application process. She stressed the need to not delay adoption of the
  ordinance. She supported allowing for Zoom access during the discussion of the Historic
  Preservation ordinance. Regarding the Commission’s ability to add items to the agenda, she
  stated that she did not know the formal procedure but that Council was explicit in their direction
  to the Commission to draft the ordinance. She did not support exclusive email communication
  and supported phone calls with a wrap up email.

  4) Veronica ALVAREZ, 1833 S. Olive Ave., questioned the purpose of the creation of the Historic
  Preservation Commission and its purpose to review items and make recommendations to
  Council. She stated that the Commission was not able to provide advice to Council regarding
  previous phases and that these recommendations were vital to the process and that the
  ordinance needed proper vetting by the Commission. She supported email communication for
  its efficacy and security. She stated that this would also allow others to be cc’d on the email
  and that the conversations could be audited if needed. She stated that the Commissioners
  needed to represent residents and advise the Council.

  5) Lewis McCAMMON, 105 N. Cordova St., distributed handouts which are on file in the City
  Clerk’s office. He discussed the background of the Historic Preservation Commission, the
  ordinance which established it, and the sections specifying the purpose of the Commission.
  He discussed the need for future addendums to Phase I or Phase II and stressed that there
  could be processes used to address concerns which would not stall progress on the ordinance.
  He discussed the need for a policy for Commissioners to add items to future agendas if there
  was unanimous consent of the Commission. He stated that while after the pandemic all Boards
  and Commissions returned to in person meetings, the Planning Commissions were accessible
  via Zoom and similar accommodations could be made for the Historic Preservation
  Commission. He supported moving public comment to the beginning of the meeting.
  4
2-10-25
   6) Ivonne Q., 123 N. Marguerita Ave., spoke regarding the need to protect Historical architecture
  in Alhambra and the structures which have been destroyed. She discussed the lengthy process
  to create the Commission and the lack of meetings held once created. She questioned why the
  City was delaying the process. She stated that Council appeared to be weakening the
  Commission’s responsibilities and that they should provide input on all aspects of the
  consultant’s work. She spoke to the expertise of the Commissioners and that they should be
  allowed to provide input on all other aspects of the Historic Preservation ordinance. She
  supported the Commissioner’s ability to draft agendas and requested a review of the
  consultant’s contract and the additional funds requested.

  7) Oscar AMARO, Ramona Park, representing the Alhambra Historic Preservation Group,
  discussed Item No. 1 on the agenda and praised Council and staff for their responses to the
  public. He stated that he was against revisiting Phase I and Phase II of the Historic Preservation
  Program. He stated that the consultants were experts in the field, clarified the request for
  contract addendum, and discussed the work of the Alhambra Historic Preservation Group. He
  stated that there had been much progress made and that he did not want to see the momentum
  halted.

  8) Melissa MICHELSON discussed Phase I and II of the Historic Preservation ordinance and
  stated that the Historic Preservation Commission did not have any input on those documents.
  She questioned the small sample size, the reason or metric of the survey, and sections of
  districts left out of the survey. She stated that her questions were unanswered and that the
  Commission was created to advise on all aspects of the ordinance. She stated that she had
  heard from other members of the public who would like more review of Phase I and II, which
  could be conducted while Council reviews the completed ordinance. She questioned comments
  made by Mr. and Mrs. Ng and their work with the consultants. She questioned Council’s
  decision to have the ordinance reviewed by the Planning Commission, and staff’s
  recommendation to not have the Historic Preservation Commission review previous phases.
  She further questioned the request for a contract addendum with the consultant and cited
  specific contract sections pertaining to cost. She further discussed her request for follow-up
  questions with staff and the need for email communication as well as her preference for email
  communication.

  9) Katie CHAN, via Zoom, requested that Council survey all former and current Board and
  Commission Members to gather direct feedback regarding the processes followed within their
  respective commissions. She went on to discuss the need for commissioners to add items to
  the agenda, to review the work of consultants, and the need to allow the Historic Preservation
  Commission to advise Council. She questioned the consultant’s request for a contract
  amendment and staff’s refusal to use email communication with commissioners.

  Discussion: Councilmember ANDRADE-STADLER recognized the passion of residents
  but also the need to pass the Historic Preservation ordinance. She commented on her own
  home and stated that there were fewer homes identified in District 5 despite the high number
  of single-family homes. She stated that the ordinance would have provisions for homeowners
  to add their homes for consideration or to opt out of the program.

  Councilmember MALONEY discussed Council’s approval of Phase I and II during this process
  and the role of the Historic Context Survey as a placeholder to review potential properties and
  provide context for the ordinance. He did not support revisiting Phase I and Phase II and
  discussed the need to move forward with the ordinance. He stated that the language used in
  the ordinance which created the Historic Preservation Commission did imply they would
  provide input on all phases of the project, but added that Council felt it was more important to
  move forward with Phase I and II while the Commission was created. He stated that the current
  Commissioners were also very involved in the earlier process as individuals. He stated that
  residents and future Commission members, as well as members of the Alhambra Preservation
  Group and the Alhambra Historic Society had direct contact with the consultant during the
  5
2-10-25
   whole process. He felt there was robust community engagement and input in the process, that
  if it were possible, Council would revise the language about the Commission’s purpose, and
  that it was best to move forward with the process. He further discussed the Commission’s
  ability to make its own agendas and stated that he did not want to see a Commission go
  beyond its scope and frustrate its purpose or intrude on the purpose of other commissions. He
  stated that there ought to be open discussion at every meeting and requested additional
  scheduled meetings for discussion and community input. He reiterated the need for efficient
  meetings, staff’s role, and the scope of Council’s direction to staff. He stated that he supported
  virtual meetings if it was possible and feasible as the commission continues to meet in Council
  Chambers. He stated that he did not feel it was necessary to broadcast regular meetings after
  the creation of the ordinance. He stated that the presiding officer of each Commission had the
  authority to accept public comment at the beginning of a meeting if necessary. He supported
  the pre-meeting calls and stated that extended emails could impact staff time. He encouraged
  verbal communication. He supported the progress made during the Historic Preservation
  Ordinance.

  Councilmember MAZA spoke to the importance of the ordinance and did not support revisiting
  Phase I and II of the project. He suggested that Commissioners could add items to the agenda
  once work on the ordinance has been completed and regular meetings take place. He agreed
  with Mr. Ng’s suggestion of recording the meetings via Zoom in Council Chambers until the
  completion of the ordinance at which time regular meetings in a conference room could
  resume. He supported public comment at the start of all board and commission meetings. He
  supported phone call communication and discussion with staff. He stated that this provided
  feedback and clarification and that they should be mindful of staff’s time. Mr. MAZA and Ms.
  BINNQUIST further discussed the contract amendment with Historic Resources Group (HRG)
  and the terms of the amendment. Mr. MAZA supported the continued public outreach included
  in the contract.

  Vice Mayor LEE discussed the importance of the Historic Preservation Commissioners and
  the pressure faced by them. She stated that while the City Council wanted the ordinance
  moved forward, that they needed to make sure that the Commission be allowed to engage in
  an intellectual debate. She stated that she expected that the Commissioners work together
  through their debates and work on their communication skills. She stated that if a
  Commissioner had a question, then the Commission should be allowed to vote on whether it
  was agendized. Ms. LEE, Ms. BINNQUIST, and City Attorney MONTES discussed the contract
  amendment with HRG, the ways it would be affected by the potential revision to Phase I or II
  of the Historic Preservation process, and staff’s request for direction from Council. Ms. LEE
  stated that she did not have an issue with Phase I and II, but would like to know the consensus
  of the Historic Preservation Commission regarding their acceptance of Phase I and II. She
  stated that she did not want Council to direct the Commission, that the Commission decision
  should not be bypassed, and that she did not agree with revisiting the previous phases of the
  project. Mr. MONTES offered clarification regarding the current commission agendas
  regarding the ordinance. Ms. LEE emphasized that she preferred the Commission to vote to
  revisit Phase I and II and that she objected to the Commission not being allowed to review the
  documents associated with Phase I and II.

  Ms. LEE stated that the Commissioners should have a similar procedure to City Council to
  add items to the agenda. She continued to discuss the role and expertise of the
  Commissioners and complaints made by former Commissioners. She stated that she did not
  have an issue with the other issues in the staff report.

  Ms. ANDRADE-STADLER reiterated that she felt Phase I and II should not be revisited due to
  Council’s previous approval based on input from the public, including individuals who were
  later appointed to the Historic Preservation Commission. She stated that the procedure to add
  items to an agenda should be revisited during the Strategic Planning Session rather than make
  6
2-10-25
   a broad decision for all commissions during this meeting. She acknowledged Ms. Lee’s
  comments regarding respecting the perspective of commissioners and added that Council has
  heard their opinions during the previous discussions as well as current public comment to
  move forward with the historic preservation ordinance.

  Mr. MAZA reiterated that the ordinance could be amended to account for any facts not
  addressed in the initial Phases of the project. He stated that the main agenda item for the
  commission should be to work on the ordinance and added that he was open to allowing the
  Commission the ability to add to their agenda once the ordinance was approved. He reiterated
  his suggestion to allow for virtual meeting access up to the approval of the ordinance. He
  clarified that the additional budgeted costs of the contract amendment with the consultant only
  applied should the Commission revisit Phase I and II. Ms. LEE stated that she did not want to
  revisit Phase I and II, but reiterated that she believed the Commission should be allowed to
  review the documents. She continued to discuss Phase II, Historic Context Survey.

  Mayor WANG agreed that it would have been a better public process to have formed the
  Commission early and allow them to engage in the first phases of the project, however she
  added that there were constraints regarding staff resources and an urgency for approval. She
  agreed with Ms. LEE that the decision should be reached by consensus of the Commission
  before coming before Council and recognized the approval of previous phases by Council.
  She stated that it was best to move forward and not delay any further. She added that
  improvements could be made in the future. Ms. WANG stated that Commissioners should be
  empowered to ask any questions to make their decisions. She stated that if the information
  was readily available it should be provided immediately to the Commission but that if the
  information required additional staff or consultant time to create, then the resources were not
  available to do so.

  Ms. WANG clarified the consensus of Council for the Historic Preservation Commission to
  move forward with Phase III of the Historic Preservation Ordinance and for staff to provide
  information that is readily available for the Commission to make an informed decision. Ms.
  WANG agreed with Ms. Andrade-Stadler that discussion of allowing Commissions to add items
  to an agenda should be during the Strategic Planning Session. She suggested a formal or
  informal survey of Commissioners to make that decision. She discussed the impact on staff
  resources to allow all Commissions to alter their agendas. Ms. WANG agreed with the
  suggestion to allow for virtual access to meetings, but added that this could also be discussed
  during Strategic Planning Session due to the impact on staff resources and any associated
  expenses. She stated that for now, audio recordings were available to the public. Ms. WANG
  stated that the Commission should decide to move public comment to the beginning of the
  meeting. Ms. WANG supported pre-meeting calls but recognized the time constraints
  available. She stated that this should be determined on an individual basis and reiterated that
  if information could be readily provided, it could be done in an email while phone calls may be
  more efficient for more complex discussions.

  Mr. MAZA and Ms. BINNQUIST discussed the cost and ability to allow virtual access to
  meetings held in Council Chambers. Ms. BINNQUIST confirmed that staff could set up Zoom
  access to the next scheduled Historic Preservation Commission meeting. Ms. ANDRADE-
  STADLER and Mr. MONTES discussed virtual meeting access and the Brown Act.

  Action Taken: City Council received and filed this report, and provided direction to staff.

CONSENT AGENDA (Item Nos. 4 – 13)

All items listed under the Consent Agenda were considered by the City Council to be routine and were
enacted by one motion.
  7
2-10-25
 4.  ACCEPT SUMMER LUNCH PROGRAM GRANT FROM THE CALIFORNIA STATE
  LIBRARY AND APPROPRIATE FUNDS – F2M25-18, M2M25-12

  The California State Library offers grants in support of library programs and pop-up visits at
  summer lunch sites to enhance access to books and library services by the community. In
  December, 2024, staff applied for this funding opportunity and was awarded $8,318 to support
  library programming at the City’s park sites participating under the free Summer Lunch
  Program. The grant funds would be used to purchase giveaway books and programming
  supplies to be used during the Library’s mobile visits during the summer.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council accepted $8,318 in grant funds from the California State
  Library to support the Library’s mobile summer programs and services; appropriated revenue
  and expenditure funds in the amount of $8,318; authorized the City Manager or designee to
  sign the grant agreement with the California State Library, subject to final language approval
  by the City Manager and City Attorney; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to
  finalize Council’s action. (M2M25-12)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  ANDRADE-STADLER, MAZA, LEE, MALONEY, WANG
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

5.  NOTICE OF COMPLETION: ALL-INCLUSIVE PLAYGROUND EQUIPMENT  FOR
  GRANADA AND ALHAMBRA PARKS – F2M24-32, C2M24-13, M2M25-13

  On February 26, 2024, the City Council awarded a contract to Landscape Structures Inc. in
  the amount of $1,199,999.49 to construct the All-Inclusive Playgrounds at Granada and
  Alhambra Parks. There were no change orders associated with the project. Staff inspected
  this project, and all work was completed in accordance with the City’s requirements and
  specifications. As such, it would be appropriate for the City Council to accept this project as
  complete.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council accepted the work of Landscape Structures Inc. for the
  All-Inclusive Playground Equipment at Granada Park and Alhambra Park as complete in the
  amount of $1,199,999.49; directed the City Clerk to file a Notice of Completion with the County
  of Los Angeles for recordation; instructed the Finance Director to release the 5 percent
  retention 35 days from the date of recordation if no liens are filed; and, directed staff to
  undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s action. (M2M25-13)

6.  RESOLUTION APPROVING A REVISED COMPREHENSIVE MEMORANDUM OF
  UNDERSTANDING (MOU) WITH THE ALHAMBRA POLICE OFFICERS’
  ASSOCIATION (APOA) – F2M25-2, R2M25-6, C87-16C, M2M25-14

  Previously, the City Council approved a revised MOU between the City and APOA on August
  26, 2024. Since then, CalPERS staff reached out to City staff regarding a need to revise certain
  language in the City and APOA’s existing MOU for compliance purposes. In particular, City
  staff complied by revising language pertaining to Drone Officer as First Responder and Acting
  Assignment as Watch Commander and Officer in Charge (Patrol). No changes were made to
  8
2-10-25
   benefits pertaining to these assignments. The changes were reviewed and approved by
  APOA.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council adopted Resolution No. R2M25-6 entitled: A Resolution
  of the Alhambra City Council approving a Revised Comprehensive Memorandum of
  Understanding between the City of Alhambra and the Alhambra Police Officers’ Association
  that incorporates California Public Employees’ Retirement System (CalPERS) required
  revisions; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s action.
  (M2M25-14)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  MALONEY
  Ayes:  ANDRADE-STADLER, MAZA, LEE, MALONEY, WANG
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

7.  RESOLUTION APPROVING A REVISED COMPREHENSIVE MEMORANDUM OF
  UNDERSTANDING (MOU) WITH THE ALHAMBRA POLICE DISPATCHERS’
  ASSOCIATION (APDA), AN AMENDED CLASS SPECIFICATION FOR DISPATCHER
AND A NEW CLASS SPECIFICATION FOR LEAD DISPATCHER – F2M25-2, C2M21-  51,
R2M25-7, M2M25-15

  Occasionally, opportunities arise that offer the ability to restructure and reorganize existing
  staffing structures in order to provide improved operations, functions and customer service.
  With Council’s approval of the new Lead Dispatcher classification, City staff could move one
  step closer to restructuring the Police Department’s Communications Division in Fiscal Year
  2025-26, to offer improved and more efficient operations and functions. These changes were
  in alignment with Goal One of the City’s Strategic Plan to “Enhance Public Safety.” A new
  Lead Dispatcher Class Specification provided Division personnel with better support. The Lead
  Dispatcher would be tasked with overseeing, training, and leading subordinate dispatchers in
  handling of calls for law enforcement and in other emergency assistance. The existing
  Dispatcher Class Specification was being amended to bring physical demand requirements to
  current standards.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council adopted Resolution No. R2M25-7 entitled: A Resolution
  of the Alhambra City Council approving a Revised Comprehensive Memorandum of
  Understanding between the City of Alhambra and the Alhambra Police Dispatchers’
  Association, an amended Class Specification for Dispatcher and a new Class Specification for
  Lead Dispatcher; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize Council’s
  action. (M2M25-15)

   In November 2020, the City Council approved a DDA with American Family Housing (AFH) to
  build a seven story 50-unit affordable housing project (Mariposa Project) on a City-owned
  parcel currently used as a surface parking lot in the downtown district between First and
  Second Streets, south of Main Street, immediately north of an AT&T Building. From 2022
  through 2024, the City Council approved an amendment clarifying the number of public parking
  spaces and five extensions to obtain all necessary construction funding including State of
  California Tax Credits. AFH did not receive tax credits and assigned the Mariposa Project to
  the Cesar Chavez Foundation (CCF). In October 2024, the City Council approved the
  proposed Assignment of the DDA to CCF. CCF is a 50-year-old non-profit organization with
  eight affordable housing projects (434 units) in the San Gabriel Valley region either in

  development costs. To make the project more competitive with 2025 State funding

  DEPARTMENT STATION 74 – F2M24-36, N2M25-15

  The roof at the Fire Department Station 74, located at 2505 W. Norwood Place, is over 20
  years old. An emergency repair to the flat roof was done last year which consisted of cleaning
  and applying a polyurethane foam to seal. Water stains on the wall were observed and there
  were also multiple broken tiles in the valleys of the roof. The recommendation was to remove
